# **(ii) Answer**

We collect five categories of financial and macroeconomic indicators to 
investigate whether euro-area monetary policy surprises can be predicted 
using previously available information.

## EURO STOXX 50

First, we use the EURO STOXX 50 equity index, obtained from Yahoo Finance using the ticker `^STOXX50E`. 

## VSTOXX

Second, we use the VSTOXX implied volatility index (`V2TX`), which measures expected volatility in the EURO STOXX 50 market. 


## ESI 

Third, we use the Economic Sentiment Indicator (ESI) for the euro area with 20 member countries. 

This is a seasonally adjusted monthly index, with a long-run reference average of 100.

## Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices

Fourth, we obtain the annual Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices inflation rate from Eurostat dataset `prc_hicp_manr`, selecting all items (`CP00`) for the euro area (`EA20`). The series is observed monthly and measured in percent.

## EURO-AREA AAA Government Bond Rates 

Finally, we use euro-area AAA government bond spot rates obtained from the ECB Data Portal for maturities of three months, six months, one year, two years, five years and ten years. 

These series are observed at daily frequency and measured in percent per annum.


## Plots

We plot the original series in levels to examine their historical behaviour before constructing the changes used as regression predictors. 

All analysis is restricted to the January 2002–October 2025 project period, subject to the historical availability of each dataset


#  **(iii) Construct $z_{t-1}$**. 
Compute the changes defined in Section 2.2 relative to the reference day $r_t$ 
of each month. Explain how you deal with weekends and holidays 
(use the last available trading day before d), 
and why no predictor uses information from the announcement day or later.

## 3-Month Cutoff FUNCTION

```{r}

# create cutoff
monthly_mps$cutoff <- monthly_mps$month_date - 1

past_change <- function(data, cutoff, val_col = 'value', h = 63, log_change = FALSE) {
  cutoff <- as.Date(cutoff)
  data_sub <- data[data$date <= cutoff & !is.na(data$date), ]
  data_sub <- data_sub[order(data_sub$date), ]
  
  vals <- as.numeric(data_sub[[val_col]])
  valid_idx <- which(!is.na(vals) & is.finite(vals))
  
  if (log_change) {
    valid_idx <- valid_idx[vals[valid_idx] > 0]
  }
  
  if (length(valid_idx) <= h) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  
  current_idx  <- valid_idx[length(valid_idx)]
  previous_idx <- valid_idx[length(valid_idx) - h]
  
  day_gap <- as.numeric(cutoff - data_sub$date[current_idx])
  if (day_gap > 7 || day_gap < 0) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  
  if (log_change) {
    return(log(vals[current_idx]) - log(vals[previous_idx]))
  }
  
  return(vals[current_idx] - vals[previous_idx])
}

```

### CUTOFF FUNCTION APPLY


```{r}


monthly_mps$stoxx_3m <- vapply(
  seq_len(nrow(monthly_mps)),
  function(i) {
    past_change(
      stoxx_cleaned,
      cutoff     = monthly_mps$cutoff[i],
      val_col    = "close",
      h          = 63,
      log_change = TRUE
    )
  },
  numeric(1)
)

monthly_mps$vstoxx_3m <- vapply(
  seq_len(nrow(monthly_mps)),
  function(i) {
    past_change(
      vstoxx_cleaned,
      cutoff     = monthly_mps$cutoff[i],
      val_col    = "level",
      h          = 63,
      log_change = FALSE
    )
  },
  numeric(1)
)

esi_cleaned$month_date <- floor_date(as.Date(esi_cleaned$date), 'month')
hicp_cleaned$month_date <- floor_date(as.Date(hicp_cleaned$date), 'month')

esi_val_col <- if ('esi' %in% names(esi_cleaned)) 'esi' else 'values'
hicp_val_col <- if ('values' %in% names(hicp_cleaned)) 'values' else 'value'

monthly_mps$esi_3m <- vapply(
  monthly_mps$month_date,
  function(d) {
    target <- as.Date(d)
    m1 <- target %m-% months(1)
    m4 <- target %m-% months(4)
    
    x1 <- esi_cleaned[[esi_val_col]][match(m1, esi_cleaned$month_date)]
    x4 <- esi_cleaned[[esi_val_col]][match(m4, esi_cleaned$month_date)]
    
    if (length(x1) == 0 || length(x4) == 0 || is.na(x1) || is.na(x4)) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }
    as.numeric(x1-x4)
  },
  numeric(1)
)

monthly_mps$inflation_3m <- NA_real_
monthly_mps$inflation_1y <- NA_real_

for (i in seq_len(nrow(monthly_mps))) {
  d <- as.Date(monthly_mps$month_date[i])
  
  m1 <- d %m-% months(1)
  m4 <- d %m-% months(4)
  m13 <- d %m-% months(13)
  
  pi1 <- hicp_cleaned[[hicp_val_col]][match(m1, hicp_cleaned$month_date)]
  pi4 <- hicp_cleaned[[hicp_val_col]][match(m4, hicp_cleaned$month_date)]
  pi13 <- hicp_cleaned[[hicp_val_col]][match(m13, hicp_cleaned$month_date)]
  
  if (length(pi1) > 0 && length(pi4) > 0 && !is.na(pi1) && !is.na(pi4)) {
    monthly_mps$inflation_3m[i] <- as.numeric(pi1-pi4)
  }
  
  if (length(pi1) > 0 && length(pi13) > 0 && !is.na(pi1) && !is.na(pi13)) {
    monthly_mps$inflation_1y[i] <- as.numeric(pi1 - pi13)
  }
}

]

monthly_mps
```

## PCA ON GOVERNMENT BOND YIELD LEVELS

```{r}

yield_pca <- prcomp(
  yield_levels[, mats],
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = FALSE
)

yield_levels$pc2 <- yield_pca$x[, 2]
yield_levels$spread <- (
  yield_levels[["10Y"]] -
    yield_levels[["3M"]]
)
if (
  cor(
    yield_levels$pc2,
    yield_levels$spread
  ) < 0
) {
  yield_levels$pc2 <- -yield_levels$pc2
}

# Verify the orientation
cor(
  yield_levels$pc2,
  yield_levels$spread
)

summary(yield_pca)
```

### WHY PC2? 
PC1 often captures common changes in the overall level of the yield curve.
PC2 often captures differences between shorter and longer maturities, corresponding to slope changes.
Because principal components are identified only up to sign, we orient PC2 to be positively correlated with the ten-year minus three-month yield spread.





## CALCULATE THE THREE MONTH PC2 CHANGE


```{r}

      h = 63,
```

# **(iii) Answer**

We construct the explanatory variables using changes in financial and macroeconomic
indicators observed prior to the corresponding ECB monetary policy surprise.
For the daily financial variables, we adopt the reference-date convention 
based on the last available trading day of the previous calendar month. 
This approach accounts for weekends and market holidays and prevents the use 
of financial observations occurring after the reference cutoff.
The STOXX and VSTOXX predictors are calculated as three-month logarithmic 
changes, using approximately 63 trading observations. The ESI predictor 
is constructed as a three-month difference in economic sentiment, while the 
inflation predictors measure three-month and twelve-month changes in the annual 
HICP inflation rate. We also perform unstandardised PCA on the daily levels 
of six euro-area government bond yields. We retain the second principal component, 
which captures an important dimension of yield-curve slope movements, and 
orient it to be positively correlated with the difference between ten-year 
and three-month government bond yields.The corresponding predictor is calculated 
as the three-month change in the oriented PC2 score. The original monetary 
policy surprise series contains 286 monthly observations between January 2002 
and October 2025. However, the available VSTOXX data cover only December 2012 
to March 2025. Consequently, we construct a common estimation sample containing 
only months for which all six predictors and the monetary policy surprise are 
available. This ensures that the regression variables are aligned by calendar 
month without artificially imputing unavailable historical observations. The 
monthly macroeconomic predictors follow the lag formulas specified in the 
assignment. Their strict real-time availability remains subject to verification
of the original publication dates, particularly for ESI and HICP inflation.

# **(iv) Answer**

Considering |r|>= 0.60 for high correlation, we conclude that only VSTOXX and STOXX, of the 
predictor pairs are highly correlated. The largest absolute correlations are 
between the two inflation measures (0.675) and between STOXX and VSTOXX changes 
(−0.673), both just above the threshold. Although not extremely-highly correlated, these 
can still increase standard errors and weaken t-statistics. 

# **(v) Estimate the Regression**. 

Regress $mps_t$ on a constant and $x_{t-1}$ by OLS. Report the estimates, 
standard errors, t-stats, $R^2$, and adjusted $R^2$, and interpret the sign of 
each coefficient (e.g. does a stock market rally before the meeting predict 
a tightening surprise?).

```{r}

reg_data <- monthly_mps %>%
  arrange(month_date) %>%
  mutate(
    lag_stoxx_3m = dplyr::lag(stoxx_3m, 1),
    lag_vstoxx_3m = dplyr::lag(vstoxx_3m, 1),
    lag_esi_3m = dplyr::lag(esi_3m, 1),
    lag_inflation_3m = dplyr::lag(inflation_3m, 1),
    lag_yield_pc2_3m = dplyr::lag(yield_pc2_3m, 1)
  )

mps_model <- lm(unstandardized ~ lag_stoxx_3m + lag_vstoxx_3m + lag_esi_3m + lag_inflation_3m + lag_yield_pc2_3m, data=reg_data)
summary(mps_model)

```

# **(v) Answer**

| Metric |  Estimates | Standard Error | T-Stat | P-Value |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Intercept | -0.003306 | 0.183678 | -0.018 | 0.986 |
| lag_stoxx_3m | -0.126226 | 2.384628 | -0.053 | 0.958 | 
| lag_esi_3m | -0.002337|  0.030533 | -0.077 | 0.939 |
| lag_inflation_3m  | 0.175668  |  0.224876   | 0.781 |   0.436| 
| lag_yield_pc2_3m  | 0.573310  | 0.512988   |1.118 |    0.265| 

 $R^2$: 0.01048, Adjusted $R^2$:  -0.008102 
 
Both lags of STOXX and ESI are slightly negative meaning an increase in either
lagged predictor corresponds to a 0.1262 & 0.002337 decrease change respectively 
in mps.The lags of Inflation and the principal component of our yield curves are both
positive meaning an increase in either lagged predictor corresponds to a 
0.175668 & 0.573310 increase change respectively in mps.
However with all covariates having extremely large p-values, we cannot
conclude that any of these four have any statistically significant predictive 
power for monetary policy tightening surprises.

# **(vi) Check the Residuals**. 

Plot the residuals and their ACF. Test for serial correlation (Ljung-Box, 
Box.test; Breusch-Godfrey, lmtest::bgtest) and for heteroscedasticity 
(Breush-Pagan, lmtest::bptest). State conclusion.

## REsid Check

```{r}

lagged_ols_resid <- resid(mps_model)
summary(lagged_ols_resid)

par(mfrow = c(1,2))
plot(lagged_ols_resid, type='l', main='OLS Residuals', ylab='Residuals')
acf(lagged_ols_resid, main='ACF of Resid.')
par(mfrow=c(1,1))

cat('Ljung-Box Test')
print(Box.test(lagged_ols_resid, type='Ljung-Box'))

cat('Breusch-Godfrey Test')
print(bgtest(mps_model))

cat('Breusch-Pagan Test')
print(bptest(mps_model))


```

# **(vi) Residual & Serial Correlation Testing**
# **(vii) Inference with HAC Standard Errors**. 

If the residuals show serial correlation or heteroscedasticity, re-estimate 
the standard errors with the Newey-West estimator 
(sandwich::NeweyWest, with the truncation lag stated, 
e.g.: $L = [4(T/100)^{2/9}]$ Compare OLS and HAC standard errors.

```{r}

n_obs <- nobs(mps_model)
L <- floor(4 * (n_obs / 100)^(2/9))
cat('Calculate Truncated Lag (L): ', L, '\n')

hac_vcov <- sandwich::NeweyWest(mps_model, lag = L, prewhite = FALSE)

cat('OLS HAC Esimates')
print(coeftest(mps_model))

cat('\n NeweyWest HAC Estimates')
print(coeftest(mps_model, vcov = hac_vcov))

se_comparison <- data.frame(
  OLS_SE = summary(mps_model)$coefficients[, 'Std. Error'],
  HAC_SE = sqrt(diag(hac_vcov))
)

cat('\n Standard Error Comparison')
print(se_comparison)

```

# **(vii) Answers**

Wtih a truncated lag of 4, we applied the NeweyWest estimator 
that attempts to correct the standard errors caused by the serial 
correlation of the residuals of our OLS model. 

Comparing the two models shows us two distinct behaviors:

When comparing the standard errors, the NeweyWest HAC standard errors are
smaller than the OLS estimators across the board. In the biggest drop off, 
we can see the standard error of our lag stoxx variable drop from 
2.38 to 1.76. 

As the standard errors of the NeweyWest estimators dropped, the t-stats
of each estimator increased in magnitude across the board as well. This
drives us to the conclusion that we are still not able to reject the null 
hypothesis for all variables despite our attempted correction. Even after 
accounting for serial correlation within the residuals, none of the lagged
predictors have statistically significant predictive power for predicting 
monetary policy surprises.


# **(viii) Test individual and joint significance**. 

Test each ${\beta}_j = 0$ and the joint hypothesis $\beta = 0$ 
(Wald test with the HAC covariance matrix, lmtest::waldtest or 
car::linearHypothesis). Is the surprise predictable?

```{r}

joint_test <- linearHypothesis(
  mps_model,
  c('lag_stoxx_3m=0', 'lag_esi_3m=0', 'lag_inflation_3m=0', 'lag_yield_pc2_3m=0'),
  vcov = hac_vcov
)

print(joint_test)

```


# **(viii) Answer**

**Individual Hypotheses ${\beta_j}=0$**

Based on the previous NeweyWest test, we failed to reject the null hypothesis
for every single predictor. The p-values for all predictor are extremely large, 
larger than our significance level of 5%. None of these lagged predictors are 
different from 0.

**Joint Hypothesis $\beta = 0$**

When conducting our linearHypothesis, we yield another large p-value of 0.4784.
This does not give us sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. We can
conclude that the variables do not have predictive power even when hypothesis 
tested together as a group.

The surprise is not predictable. Using this model, both the individual and joint
tests conclude that the lagged predictors we used have no statistically significant
power in predicting this event. These surprises, as the name states, are completely
independent from the dataset we have chosen.

# **(ix) Robustness Check**. 

Re-estimate with 
(a) different horizons for the market variables (1 day, 1 month),
(b) only the months with an announcement (dropping the months with $mps_t = 0$), 
(c) the yield-curve spread instead of PC2, and 
(d) excluding the 2008-2009 crisis or the 2020 COVID period. Do the conclusions change?

## (a)

```{r}

monthly_mps$stoxx_1m <- vapply(
  seq_len(nrow(monthly_mps)),
  function(i) past_change(stoxx_cleaned, cutoff=monthly_mps$cutoff[i],
                          val_col='close', h=21, log_change = TRUE),
  numeric(1)
)

yield_levels <- yield_levels %>% mutate(spread = `10Y` - `2Y`)
monthly_mps$yield_spread_1m <- vapply(
  seq_len(nrow(monthly_mps)),
  function(i) past_change(yield_levels, cutoff=monthly_mps$cutoff[i],
                          val_col = 'spread', h=21, log_change= FALSE),
  numeric(1)
)

monthly_mps$esi_1m <- vapply(
  monthly_mps$month_date,
  function (d) { 
    target <- as.Date(d)
    m1 <- target %m-% months(1)
    m2 <- target %m-% months(2)
    x1 <- esi_cleaned[[esi_val_col]][match(m1, esi_cleaned$month_date)]
    x2 <- esi_cleaned[[esi_val_col]][match(m2, esi_cleaned$month_date)]
    
    if (length(x1) == 0 || length(x2) == 0 || is.na(x1) || is.na(x2)) return(NA_real_)
    as.numeric(x1 - x2)
        },
  numeric(1)
)

monthly_mps$inflation_1m <- NA_real_
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(monthly_mps))) {
      d <- as.Date(monthly_mps$month_date[i])
      m1 <- d %m-% months(1)
      m2 <- d %m-% months(2)
      
      pi1 <- hicp_cleaned[[hicp_val_col]][match(m1, hicp_cleaned$month_date)]
      pi2 <- hicp_cleaned[[hicp_val_col]][match(m2, hicp_cleaned$month_date)]
      
      if (length(pi1) > 0 && length(pi2) > 0 && !is.na(pi1) && !is.na(pi2)) {
        monthly_mps$inflation_1m[i] <- as.numeric(pi1- pi2)
      }
    }

reg_data_1m <- monthly_mps %>%
  arrange(month_date) %>%
  mutate(
    lag_stoxx_1m = lag(stoxx_1m, 1),
    lag_esi_1m = lag(esi_1m, 1),
    lag_inflation_1m = lag(inflation_1m, 1),
    lag_yield_spread = lag(yield_spread_1m, 1)
    ) %>%
  filter(unstandardized != 0) %>%
  filter(!format(as.Date(month_date), '%Y') %in% c('2008', '2009', '2020')) %>%
  drop_na(unstandardized, lag_stoxx_1m, lag_esi_1m, lag_inflation_1m, lag_yield_spread)

mps_model_1m <- lm(unstandardized ~ lag_stoxx_1m + lag_esi_1m + lag_inflation_1m + lag_yield_spread, data= reg_data_1m)

T_obs_1m <- nobs(mps_model_1m)
L_1m <- floor(4 * (T_obs_1m / 100)^(2/9))
hac_vcov_1m <- sandwich::NeweyWest(mps_model_1m, lag = L_1m, prewhite=FALSE)

se_comparison_1m <- data.frame(
  OLS_SE_1_MONTH = summary(mps_model_1m)$coefficients[, 'Std. Error'],
  HAC_SE_1_MONTH = sqrt(diag(hac_vcov_1m))
)

cat('\n Standard Error Comparison of 1 Month Horizon Models')
print(se_comparison_1m)

```

After setting our time horizon to just 1 month, we ran the exact same NeweyWest 
test to see how our estimators adjusted their standard errors.

We see slightly different behavior to our 3 month horizon model as our standard
errors actually increased. STOXX increased from 4.93 to 6.77 and the yield curve
from 1.67 to 1.83. Our macroeconomic variables had their standard errors decrease,
similar to our 3-month baseline model. 

But as our standard errors for our financial variables increased, the t-statistics
would theoretically increase their p-values, making their predictive power less
statistically significant. This overall test reinforces our initial findings 
that this set of predictors have no predictive power for monetary event shocks.

## (b)


```{r}

reg_data_meetings_only <- reg_data %>%
  filter(unstandardized != 0)

model_meetings_only <- lm(unstandardized ~ lag_stoxx_3m + lag_esi_3m + lag_inflation_3m + lag_yield_pc2_3m, data=reg_data_meetings_only)

T_obs_meetings_only <- nobs(model_meetings_only)
L_meetings_only <- floor(4 * (T_obs_meetings_only / 100)^(2/9))
hac_vcov_meetings_only <- sandwich::NeweyWest(model_meetings_only, lag=L_meetings_only, prewhite=FALSE)

se_comparison_meetings_only <- data.frame(
  OLS_SE_MEETINGS_ONLY = summary(model_meetings_only)$coefficients[, 'Std. Error'],
  HAC_SE_1_MEETINGS_ONLY = sqrt(diag(hac_vcov_meetings_only))
)

cat('\n Standard Error Comparison of 1 Month Horizon Models')
print(se_comparison_meetings_only)
```

After filtering out any instances without an accompanying meeting, we can see 
yet again trivial differences in standard errors, but no real change to our
overarching conclusions. The standard errors of the HAC model are smaller
across the board when compared with the OLS model. But these differences are
much smaller than observed in prior instances. This is induced by the sample
size penalty of pruning any observation without a monetary meeting occurring 
that month. We still conclude that our subset of predictors have no 
statistically significant predictive power for monetary event surprises.

## (c)

```{r}

yield_levels <- yield_levels %>% mutate(spread = `10Y` - `2Y`)
monthly_mps$yield_spread_3m <- vapply(
  seq_len(nrow(monthly_mps)),
  function(i) past_change(yield_levels, cutoff=monthly_mps$cutoff[i],
                          val_col='spread', h=63, log_change=FALSE),
  numeric(1)
)

reg_data_cd <- monthly_mps %>%
  arrange(month_date) %>%
  mutate(
    lag_stoxx_3m = lag(stoxx_3m, 1),
    lag_esi_3m = lag(esi_3m, 1),
    lag_inflation_3m = lag(inflation_3m, 1),
    lag_yield_spread_3m = lag(yield_spread_3m, 1)
  ) %>% 
  drop_na(unstandardized, lag_stoxx_3m, lag_esi_3m, lag_inflation_3m, lag_yield_spread_3m)

model_cd <- lm(unstandardized ~ lag_stoxx_3m + lag_esi_3m + lag_inflation_3m + yield_spread_3m, data=reg_data_cd)
T_obs_cd <- nobs(model_cd)
L_cd <- floor(4 * (T_obs_cd / 100)^(2/9))
hac_vcov_cd <- sandwich::NeweyWest(model_cd, lag=L_cd, prewhite=FALSE)

print(coeftest(model_cd, vcov = hac_vcov_cd))

```

Results of HAC standard Errors still par for the course. All predictors have
too large of p-values to be statistically significant. Swapping in the yield curve
for PC2 yields no distinct change in predictive power. This test yet again 
reinforces our initial findings that this set of predictors have no predictive
power for monetary event shocks.

## (d)

```{r}

reg_data_pruned <- monthly_mps %>%
  arrange(month_date) %>%
  mutate(
    lag_stoxx_3m = lag(stoxx_3m, 1),
    lag_esi_3m = lag(esi_3m, 1),
    lag_inflation_3m = lag(inflation_3m, 1),
    lag_yield_spread_3m = lag(yield_spread_3m, 1)
  ) %>% 
  drop_na(unstandardized, lag_stoxx_3m, lag_esi_3m, lag_inflation_3m, lag_yield_spread_3m) %>%
  filter(!format(as.Date(month_date), '%Y') %in% c('2008', '2009', '2020')) %>%
  drop_na(unstandardized, lag_stoxx_3m, lag_esi_3m, lag_inflation_3m, lag_yield_spread_3m)

pruned_model <- lm(unstandardized ~ lag_stoxx_3m + lag_esi_3m + lag_inflation_3m + lag_yield_spread_3m, data=reg_data_pruned)

T_obs_pruned <- nobs(pruned_model)
L_pruned <- floor(4* T_obs_pruned / 100)^(2/9)
hac_vcov_pruned <- sandwich::NeweyWest(pruned_model, lag=L_pruned, prewhite=FALSE)

print(coeftest(pruned_model, vcov=hac_vcov_pruned))

```

Even after pruning out all years containing massive market crashes and rallies,
p-values for all predictors remain too large for our significance level. From
several of our robustness checks, our model cannot improve the predictability 
of any of the predictors and thus cannot capture any inference to when a
shock may occur after monetary events.
